_comment: THE NODE PAYLOAD: `nodes.NodeView`, the one object `nodes.list`, `nodes.wake`,
`nodes.sleep` and the `node.state_changed` event all carry, and the three
things every reader of it re-derives BY HAND.
There are five independent readers. services/hub/internal/nodes/view.go
PRODUCES it; apps/desktop/.../lib/remoteNodes.ts, apps/tui/src/nodes.rs and
the inline client in services/hub/cmd/hub/mobile.html each re-declare the
state vocabulary, the `signal-` prefix rule and the cost sentence in their
own language, and webBackend.ts / ipc.ts pass the object through untouched.
Nothing pinned them to each other until this file.
IT HAD ALREADY BITTEN, ONCE, BEFORE THIS FILE EXISTED. The sleep path added
a FIFTH state (`stopping`) and two wire fields (`sleptByHub`,
`mayBeRunning`) and merged. It reached the hub, the desktop and /m; the TUI
still coerces `stopping` to `unreachable`, which paints a machine somebody
deliberately told to stop with the warning marker and offers to start it
again. Every client's unknown-state fallback is individually correct and
well-argued. What was missing was anything that TELLS the person adding a
sixth state that four clients will silently mislabel it.
The `signal-` rule is the sharper edge of the same problem: that string is
produced by a shell printf in deploy/fly/node/entrypoint.sh and re-parsed by
four independent startsWith checks. Spell it `sigterm` on either side and
every client reports a clean sleep as a crash, loudly, forever.
THE BLOCK REGISTRY. Every array-of-objects block in this file must be
declared here and everything here must be a block — closure in both
directions. Held by cmd/brain/corpusvocab_test.go and
apps/desktop/src/main/services/contractsVocabulary.test.ts.

states.why: The state vocabulary itself: the five strings a NodeView.state may hold, whether each one reads as work in progress, and whether a client offers an ENABLED wake control in it. The hub-side loader checks only the vocabulary (State.Valid) — `wakeOffered` is a CLIENT rule and the hub deliberately does not share it: Supervisor.Wake accepts a wake mid-`stopping` on purpose (it abandons the stop, because the thing somebody just asked for wins). The clients' job is not to invite that race, not to make it impossible.

lastExit.cases.why: One `lastExit.reason` and the verdict every reader must reach from it: `clean` is the hub's ExitRecord.Clean(), and `notice` is whether a client puts a crash line on the row. The rule is a PREFIX TEST on a string a shell wrote, which is why the near-miss spellings are pinned beside the real ones.

presentation.cases.why: How each state is PRESENTED, per client. `fallbackDetail` is the one string that must be byte-identical everywhere it appears (the desktop and /m both ship it verbatim); the chip labels deliberately differ — /m drops the ellipsis, the TUI is lower-case house style — so they are pinned per copy rather than merged. A null `tui*` triple means THIS CLIENT HAS NOT BEEN TAUGHT THE STATE YET, and the Rust loader then asserts the documented fallback (coerce to Unreachable) instead of a presentation. That is what makes a fifth state a failing test on the client that skipped it rather than a quiet mislabelling.

states.why: Its provider is on the bus and answering. There is nothing to start, so no client shows the control at all — a visible-but-dead button is the failure class this whole feature exists to remove.

The hub asked the cloud API to start the machine and is waiting for the provider to register. Bounded and intentional, so it reads as progress; the control is VISIBLE and disabled rather than hidden, because a control that vanishes mid-action reads as a click that did nothing.

The sleep path's mirror of `waking`, and the state that proved this fixture was needed. A machine takes real seconds to drain; rendering that as `unreachable` turns a deliberate act into a warning, and offering an enabled Connect beside a disabled 'Shutting down…' puts two buttons that fight each other on one row. The transition owns the row until it settles.

Switched off, deliberately, and one button away. This is the state the whole package exists to separate from `unreachable`: collapsing 'asleep on purpose' into 'broken' is what makes a remote node feel broken to use.

The hub does not know how to get a working node out of this, and a person should look. A wake is still offered because it is the one action that can help, and because this state also covers a machine that is RUNNING and providing nothing. It is also the mandated coercion target for any state string a client does not recognise.

_comment: `clean`  — the hub's ExitRecord.Clean(): did this ending read as a
deliberate stop? Anything unrecognised is NOT clean, which is
the direction that errs toward telling the user to look.
`notice` — does a client render the crash line? It is not simply !clean:
a MISSING record means nobody knows, and saying nothing is not
the same as reassuring somebody.

cases.name: a deliberate stop, SIGTERM
cases.why: The ordinary sleep. This is what the entrypoint writes when the hub's stop lands, and every client must stay silent about it.

cases.name: a deliberate stop, SIGINT
cases.why: node/fly.toml sets kill_signal = SIGINT, so this is the spelling a PLATFORM stop produces. A reader that recognised only signal-TERM would report every platform-initiated sleep as a crash.

cases.name: the prefix is the whole rule, so signal-KILL is clean too
cases.why: Pinned because it is surprising and because it is what the code does: the test is HasPrefix, not a list of graceful signals. A reader that special-cased KILL as a crash would disagree with the other three on a record they all receive.

cases.name: the near-miss spelling is NOT a deliberate stop
cases.why: THE FAILURE THIS BLOCK EXISTS FOR. The reason string is produced by a shell printf on the node and re-parsed by four independent startsWith checks. Drop or rename the prefix on the writing side and every client flips a clean sleep into a crash notice, on every row, forever.

cases.name: case is not folded
cases.why: Go's HasPrefix, JavaScript's startsWith and Rust's starts_with are all byte-exact, so all three agree here — and they must keep agreeing if anyone is tempted to lower-case one side.

cases.name: claudemon died under it
cases.why: One of the entrypoint's own words for a failure. 137 is the OOM shape, and the exit code has to survive to the row: 'it died' and 'it was killed for memory' are different next actions.

cases.name: the brain died under it
cases.why: The other half: the machine was fine and the thing that makes it a NODE was not. It is the case where the cloud API says `stopped` and means something entirely different from sleep.

cases.name: it never got up
cases.why: The crash-loop shape. Fly's on-failure policy retries and then leaves the machine `stopped`, byte-for-byte identical over the API to a healthy sleeper; this record is one of the three things that tell them apart.

cases.name: the entrypoint could not say why
cases.why: THE UNKNOWN-REASON CASE. The entrypoint writes this literal word when it cannot classify the ending, and it must land as a crash rather than as silence — an ending nobody can account for is the one most worth a person's attention.

cases.name: a reason nobody has coined yet
cases.why: The forward-compatible half of the same rule: a reason a client has never seen is a crash, not a shrug. This is what lets the entrypoint grow a new word without a client release.

cases.name: no record at all
cases.why: ABSENT MEANS NOBODY KNOWS, and it is most of the time — the file lives on the node's volume, so the hub cannot read it while the node is off. Not clean, and no notice either: a client that rendered a crash line here would warn about every node it has not yet seen up.

cases.name: a record with an empty reason
cases.why: The same answer by a different road: a record whose reason did not survive is not an account of anything, so it is not clean and it is not worth a sentence.

_comment: `fallbackDetail` is the sentence a client shows when the hub sent no
`detail` of its own. It is BYTE-IDENTICAL on the desktop and /m today and
must stay that way; the TUI's is its own lower-case copy.
A null tuiLabel/tuiMarker/tuiFallbackDetail is a DECLARED GAP, not a
blank to fill in later with anything. It says this client coerces the
state to `unreachable`, and the Rust loader asserts exactly that — so the
commit that teaches the TUI the state fails until it fills these in.

cases.fallbackDetail: This machine is on the bus and answering.
cases.tuiFallbackDetail: this machine is on the bus and answering.
cases.why: The only state with no control on the row at all.

cases.fallbackDetail: The machine is booting — usually ready in about 20 seconds.
cases.tuiFallbackDetail: the machine is booting — usually ready in about 20 seconds.
cases.why: The BUSY tone, never a warning: it is the same tone a thinking agent uses, and it is what keeps a booting machine from reading as a broken one. The ~20s figure is in the copy on purpose — a wait with a number is a wait people sit through.

cases.fallbackDetail: The machine is shutting down cleanly. It stops billing once it is off.
cases.tuiFallbackDetail: the machine is shutting down cleanly. it stops billing once it is off.
cases.why: THE GAP THIS FIXTURE OPENED, NOW CLOSED. The sleep path shipped this state to the hub, the desktop and /m and not to the TUI, which coerced it to `unreachable` — the warning marker, the 'can't reach' chip and an offer to start a machine in the middle of stopping. The TUI learned it, so the nulls that made that omission a failing assertion are filled in. The marker is the mirrored half of `waking`'s, filling the other way, because a machine draining on purpose is busy and not broken.

cases.fallbackDetail: Switched off, and nothing is billing. Connecting will start it.
cases.tuiFallbackDetail: switched off, and nothing is billing. waking will start it.
cases.why: MUTED, not a warning: this is the state a node is SUPPOSED to spend most of its life in, and painting it as a problem is how the feature would have felt broken by design.

cases.fallbackDetail: The hub can't get a working machine out of this one.
cases.tuiFallbackDetail: the hub can't get a working machine out of this one.
cases.why: The one state that is a warning, and the coercion target for anything unrecognised. Its wording is deliberately about the HUB's inability rather than the machine's condition, because it covers both a machine that is off and broken and one that is up and providing nothing.
